From Hotel: 1h 15min → Mission San Juan Capistrano
1. Mission San Juan Capistrano
Founded 1776 — the "Jewel of the Missions," famed for its returning swallows and the dramatic ruins of the 1806 Great Stone Church, toppled by an 1812 earthquake. The Serra Chapel is California's oldest building still in use; an audio tour winds through gardens and adobe.

2. Heisler Park
A bluff-top park along Laguna's shoreline — paved paths above tide pools, palm-framed Pacific overlooks, public sculpture, and stairs down to Divers Cove. The marine-protected coves below hold some of Southern California's clearest water; sunset here is the town's ritual.

3. Laguna Village
Laguna's walkable downtown — Forest Avenue's galleries and pocket courtyards lead down to Main Beach, where a boardwalk, lawn, and lifeguard tower meet the sand. An artists' colony since the 1910s; the village stroll itself is the draw.

Heads Up
The Getty Villa — Reach it via PCH only
After the Palisades fire the Sunset Blvd approach stays closed; only Pacific Coast Highway reaches the Villa, through a 25 mph zone.
Disneyland — Reservation and ticket must match
A dated ticket alone is not enough on busy days; the park reservation and the dated ticket must be for the same park, booked separately.

Worth Knowing

The Man Who Funded This Observatory Shot His Wife and Went to Prison

Griffith Observatory exists because a convicted felon spent his final years trying to buy back a reputation he'd destroyed. Griffith J. Griffith, the mining magnate who'd already donated the land that became Griffith Park, shot his wife in a Santa Monica hotel room in 1903 during an alcohol-fueled paranoid episode, permanently disfiguring her and costing her an eye. He served nearly two years in San Quentin. After his release, he tried to fund an observatory and planetarium for the city as a gesture of civic redemption — and the city refused to take his money, unwilling to be associated with an ex-convict. Griffith left the funds in his will instead, and only after his death did Los Angeles finally accept the gift, eventually building the observatory that opened in 1935 and still offers free public telescope viewing most clear nights.

The Blue Boy caused something close to a national outcry in Britain when Henry Huntington bought it in 1921 for what was then the highest price ever paid for a painting. The sale, coming so soon after the First World War, was widely read in England as a symbol of American wealth eclipsing British cultural power, and before the painting could leave the country the National Gallery in London staged a farewell exhibition that drew enormous crowds. The gallery's director wrote "au revoir" on the back of the canvas, hoping it might someday come home. It did — briefly, exactly one century later — before returning to hang in the gallery that now sits inside the Huntington's grounds.
